title: Company Policies and Rules That Are Too Specific Can Replace Sound Judgment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on Mary Barra's reform at GM, this piece argues that overly prescriptive policies invite people to live down to rules rather than up to principles. Barra replaced a 10-page dress code with Dress Appropriately, and norms elevated once expectations became general and trusted judgment became required. While certain areas (safety, compliance, financial controls) require precise rules, many organizational domains (customer relationships, team interaction, performance management) function better with broad principles. Specific rules gain compliance; smart principles gather commitment.
points: People live down to overly prescriptive policies, following bare minimums; broad principles invite judgment, ownership, and behavior exceeding minimums.
Mary Barras Dress Appropriately policy elevated norms at GM by requiring employees to interpret intent and apply judgment thoughtfully.
Safety, compliance, regulatory, and financial policies must be precise; but customer service, interviews, and performance management often work better with general guidelines.
Hyper-detailed customer service scripts (3-ring answer time, exact greeting, limited help types) create compliance but robotic responses and lower satisfaction.
Smart principles require employees to think, make sound judgments, and decide how to meet expectations, resulting in more thoughtful, human responses.
quotes: In her view, people live down to overly prescriptive policies. In other words, people push the boundaries and fight against the rules by doing exactly whats required.

By contrast, broad principles or guidelines invite judgment, ownership, and high standards. People live up to them. Instead of following a script, people must interpret the intent of the rule and apply it thoughtfully.
Tight rules gain compliance, but smart principles gather commitment. The specifics of rules and policies shape behavior.

Examine the many rules and policies in your organization and team. Are any so specific as to create hidden resistance and thoughtlessness?” Archived from Admired Leadership Newsletter on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
